entry: Austrian composer and violinist known as the "Waltz King." Strauss composed over 500 [[Waltz|waltzes]], polkas, quadrilles, marches and other dance music, as well as several operettas and a ballet. His best-known works include "The Blue Danube," "Kaiser-Walzer" (Emperor Waltz), "Tales from the Vienna Woods" and "Frühlingsstimmen" (Voices of Spring). Among his operettas, *Die Fledermaus* and *Der Zigeunerbaron* are the best known. His father, the composer Johann Strauss I, wanted him to become a banker, and he studied the violin in secret. In October 1844 he made his debut at Dommayer's Casino in Hietzing, a suburb of [[Vienna]]. His brothers Josef and Eduard also became composers of light music.

German polymath regarded as the most influential writer in the German language. A poet, playwright, novelist, scientist, statesman and critic, Goethe wrote works including plays, poetry and aesthetic criticism, as well as treatises on [[Botany|botany]], [[Anatomy|anatomy]] and color. His first novel, *The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774), brought him fame, and he settled in Weimar in 1775, where he served the court of Duke Karl August. In 1794 he began a friendship with the dramatist [[Friedrich Schiller]], and together they are associated with Weimar Classicism. His most celebrated [[Drama|drama]], *Faust*, appeared in part in 1808. His first major scientific work was the *Metamorphosis of Plants*. The German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer named *Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship* one of the four greatest novels ever written, and many composers, including Ludwig van Beethoven and Franz Schubert, set his [[Poetry|poems]] to music.

German composer and pianist of the mid-Romantic period. His works include four symphonies, four concertos, a Requiem, much [[Chamber music|chamber music]], and hundreds of folk-song arrangements and Lieder (German art songs). Born in Hamburg to a musical family, he toured Central Europe as a pianist and met [[Franz Liszt]] in Weimar. Through Joseph Joachim he gained the support of [[Robert Schumann]] and his wife, [[Clara Schumann]], with whom he remained a close friend after Robert's death. Brahms never married. He worked in [[Vienna]], where he led the Singakademie and the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde. He was deemed conservative in the War of the Romantics. [[Arnold Schoenberg]] stressed the progressive structural coherence of his music, and his works remain a staple of the concert repertoire.

Dutch theoretical physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1910 "for his work on the equation of state for gases and liquids." He began as a schoolteacher and became the first physics professor of the University of [[Amsterdam]] in 1877. He is best known for the van der Waals equation, which describes the behavior of gases and their condensation to the liquid phase. His 1873 thesis noted the non-ideality of real gases and attributed it to intermolecular interactions, and his equation accounted for the finite volume of [[Molecule|molecules]]. The forces between stable molecules are named for him: [[Van der Waals force|van der Waals forces]]. His work influenced Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, who first liquefied helium in 1908, a step that led directly to his 1911 discovery of [[Superconductivity|superconductivity]].

German astronomer and mathematician who was a key figure of the [[Scientific Revolution]]. He is best known for three laws of planetary motion, published in *Astronomia nova* (1609) and *Harmonices Mundi* (1619). The first two laws state that planets follow elliptical paths with the Sun at one focus, and that a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. The third law relates the square of a planet's orbital period to the cube of its semi-major axis. Kepler worked as an assistant to [[Tycho Brahe]], whose observations of Mars he used, and later as imperial mathematician in Prague. His *Astronomiae Pars Optica* (1604) described how lenses form images, and he invented an improved version of the [[Telescope|refracting telescope]]. He was also an astrologer, and his novel *Somnium* earned him the description "father of science fiction."

Dutch painter of domestic interior scenes of middle-class life, one of the greatest painters of the Dutch Golden Age. Vermeer spent his life in Delft, where he was a moderately successful genre painter and earned his living partly as an art dealer. He produced relatively few paintings, worked slowly and used expensive pigments, and is renowned for his use of light. Many of his works show the same rooms and furniture in different arrangements. He was not wealthy, and at his death his wife was left in debt. His reputation declined after his death, and he was omitted from major surveys of Dutch art for nearly two centuries. He was rediscovered in the 19th century, and only 34 paintings are universally attributed to him today. His best-known works include *Girl with a Pearl Earring* and *The Milkmaid*. He may have used a [[Camera obscura|camera obscura]] to achieve his optical precision.

Largest city in South Africa and capital of [[Gauteng]] province (pop., 2022: 4,803,262). Founded in 1886 after gold was discovered on the Witwatersrand, the city grew to more than 100,000 people within a decade. It is the seat of the Constitutional Court, although [[Bloemfontein]] is the official judicial capital. Johannesburg is the economic center of the country and home to the continent's largest [[Stock exchange|stock exchange]]. Under apartheid, Soweto was designated for Black residents, and it became the center of the [[Soweto uprising|Soweto Uprising]] of 1976, when student protests were met with violent force. [[Nelson Mandela]] and [[Desmond Tutu]] were among the anti-apartheid leaders who lived there. Formerly white-only areas include Sandton, known as "Africa's richest square-mile."

First prime minister of [[Canada]] and a leading figure in Confederation. Macdonald was born in Scotland and emigrated with his family to Kingston, in Upper Canada, as a boy. He entered politics in 1844 and became premier of the Province of Canada in 1857. In 1864 he agreed to a Great Coalition with his rival George Brown to seek federation, and he was a leading figure in the conferences that produced the British North America Act and the establishment of Canada on July 1, 1867. He served as prime minister from 1867 to 1873 and again from 1878 until his death. His government established the North-West Mounted Police and brought [[British Columbia]] and [[Prince Edward Island]] into the country. He resigned in 1873 over a scandal involving bribes from businessmen seeking the Canadian Pacific Railway contract. Critics have pointed to his role in the Chinese head tax and in federal policies toward Indigenous peoples. He approved the execution of [[Louis Riel]] in 1885, which alienated many francophones.

Founding Father and second president of the United States, serving from 1797 to 1801. As a Massachusetts delegate to the Continental Congress, he seconded the Lee Resolution and helped draft the Declaration of Independence. He was vice president under [[George Washington]] before he was elected president as a Federalist. His insistence on neutrality in the French Revolutionary Wars drew criticism from both Jeffersonian Republicans and his own party. He lost his 1800 reelection bid to his former friend [[Thomas Jefferson]]. He and his son [[John Quincy Adams]], the sixth president, were the only presidents of the first twelve who never owned slaves.

American psychologist who popularized the scientific theory of [[Behaviorism|behaviorism]] and established it as a psychological school. Watson advanced the discipline through his 1913 address at [[Columbia University]], "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It." His behaviorist approach encompassed research on animal behavior, child rearing and advertising. He is known for the controversial "Little Albert" experiment, in which an infant was conditioned to fear a white rat. He edited the *Psychological Review* from 1910 to 1915. A 2002 survey ranked him the 17th most cited psychologist of the 20th century. Watson taught at [[Johns Hopkins University]] until he resigned in 1920 following a public scandal over his affair with his research assistant, Rosalie Rayner, whom he later married. He then worked in advertising and wrote child-rearing advice.

American physicist and electrical engineer, the only person to win the Nobel Prize in Physics twice. He shared the 1956 prize with Walter Brattain and [[William Shockley]] for the invention of the [[Transistor|transistor]], and the 1972 prize with Leon Cooper and John Robert Schrieffer for the BCS theory of [[Superconductivity|superconductivity]]. He worked at [[Bell Labs]] after [[World War II]] and later taught at the University of Illinois. The transistor made possible almost every modern electronic device and ushered in the [[Information Age]]. Bardeen's superconductivity work is used in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and medical magnetic resonance imaging. Born and raised in Wisconsin, he earned a Ph.D. in physics from [[Princeton University]].

American comedian and actor, one of the original cast members of [[Saturday Night Live]]. Born in [[Chicago]] to Albanian-American parents, Belushi performed with The Second City before joining the show in its first season. He created characters including Henry Kissinger and Ludwig van Beethoven. He appeared in *National Lampoon's Animal House* (1978) and co-founded the Blues Brothers with [[Dan Aykroyd]], an act that led to the film *The Blues Brothers* (1980). He died at age 33 from a lethal mixture of heroin and cocaine at the Chateau Marmont in Hollywood. Cathy Smith was convicted of involuntary manslaughter in his death.

American abolitionist who advocated violence to end slavery. An evangelical Christian, Brown believed he was an instrument of God. He first drew national attention during Bleeding Kansas, where in May 1856 he and his sons killed five supporters of slavery in the Pottawatomie massacre. In October 1859 he led a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, hoping to start a slave insurrection. Seven people were killed. Brown was tried for treason and hanged on December 2, 1859. His raid escalated tensions that led to the [[American Civil War]] the following year. He was widely viewed as a hero in the North.

American composer, visual artist and music theorist and a leading figure of the post-war avant-garde. A pioneer of indeterminacy and chance in music, Cage studied Indian philosophy and [[Zen]] in the late 1940s and began composing chance-controlled music in 1951. The [[I Ching]] became his standard composition tool. His best-known work, *4′33″* (1952), is performed in the absence of deliberate sound, so that the ambient sounds of the environment become its content. He was also a pioneer of the prepared piano, for which he wrote *Sonatas and Interludes* (1946–48). He studied with [[Arnold Schoenberg]] and was instrumental in the development of [[Modern dance|modern dance]] through his association with choreographer Merce Cunningham.

French theologian and reformer in Geneva, the principal figure in the development of Calvinism. Originally trained as a humanist lawyer, he broke from the [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic Church]] around 1530. After religious violence against Protestants in France, he fled to [[Basel]], where in 1536 he published the first edition of his *Institutes of the Christian Religion*. That year he joined the Reformation in [[Geneva]], but the city council expelled him and William Farel. He worked in [[Strasbourg]] and returned to Geneva in 1541, where he introduced new forms of church government and liturgy. His doctrines of [[Predestination]] and God's absolute sovereignty shaped Reformed churches, including [[Presbyterianism]], that spread throughout the world. He wrote commentaries on most books of the Bible. In 1553 the city council burned Michael Servetus at the stake for heresy after Calvin denounced him.

Canadian actor and comedian best known for his work in Hollywood comedy films. He first rose to prominence in the 1970s with the [[Toronto]] branch of The Second City. In the 1980s he starred in films including *Splash* (1984), *Planes, Trains and Automobiles* (1987) and *Uncle Buck* (1989), and he had supporting roles in *Home Alone* (1990). He co-owned the Toronto Argonauts of the Canadian Football League. Candy died of a heart attack in 1994, at age 43, while filming *Wagons East*. The film and the completed *Canadian Bacon* (1995) were released posthumously.

American filmmaker, composer and actor, recognized as a master of the [[Horror film|horror]] genre. Carpenter is best known for horror, action and science fiction films of the 1970s and 1980s, including *Halloween* (1978), *Escape from New York* (1981) and *The Thing* (1982). Many of his other productions were initially overlooked and later became cult classics, among them *Assault on Precinct 13* (1976) and *They Live* (1988). He usually composes or co-composes the music for his films. He won the Golden Coach Award at the 2019 [[Cannes Film Festival]], and in 2025 he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

American independent filmmaker and actor who helped pioneer modern American independent cinema. He began as a television and film actor and received a nomination for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *The Dirty Dozen* (1967). As a director, he often self-financed his films, which used an improvisational style and a cinéma vérité feel. His works include *Shadows* (1959), *Faces* (1968) and *A Woman Under the Influence* (1974), which earned him Academy Award nominations for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay. He was married to actress [[Gena Rowlands]] until his death, and they frequently collaborated.

American actor and former professional wrestler and rapper. Born in [[Massachusetts]], Cena wrestled for [[WWE]] for 24 years and became a record-setting 17-time world champion. He held the WWE Championship a record 14 times. He released the rap album *You Can't See Me* (2005) and began acting in 2006. He starred in films including *Trainwreck* (2015), *Blockers* (2018) and *The Suicide Squad* (2021), and he portrayed the title character in the series *Peacemaker*. He has granted more than 650 wishes for the Make-A-Wish Foundation, the most in the organization's history.

Church Father and archbishop of [[Constantinople]], known for his preaching and public speaking. Born in [[Antioch]], he studied [[Rhetoric|rhetoric]] under Libanius and later theology under Diodorus of Tarsus. From 386 to 397 he preached at Antioch's cathedral, and his eloquence earned him the name John the Golden-mouthed. He emphasized charitable giving and the needs of the poor. Appointed archbishop of Constantinople in 397 or 398, he denounced clerical abuses and court extravagance, which led to his deposition in 403. He was exiled and died during forced marches. He is honored as a saint in the Catholic and Eastern churches and is one of the Three Holy Hierarchs with [[Basil of Caesarea]] and [[Gregory of Nazianzus]]. His Divine Liturgy is still used in Eastern Christianity.

British army officer and statesman who is known for never having lost a battle. From a gentry family, Churchill served as a page at the court of James, Duke of York, in the 1670s. His role in the Monmouth Rebellion of 1685 helped secure James on the throne, but he took part in the conspiracy that led to James's deposition in the [[Glorious Revolution]]. Charges of [[Jacobitism]] led to his temporary imprisonment in the [[Tower of London]]. After the accession of Queen Anne in 1702 he became captain-general of British forces and de facto leader of Allied forces in the Low Countries. His victories at Blenheim (1704), Ramillies (1706), Oudenarde (1708) and Malplaquet (1709) secured his place among Europe's great generals. He was forced from office amid Tory and Whig rivalries, and a stroke in 1716 ended his career. His campaigns against [[Louis XIV]] helped establish Britain as a front-rank power.

English comedian and actor, a founding member of [[Monty Python]]. Emerging from the Cambridge Footlights in the 1960s, Cleese cofounded the surreal sketch comedy troupe, whose films include *Monty Python and the Holy Grail* (1975) and *Life of Brian* (1979). He cowrote and starred in the sitcom [[Fawlty Towers]], playing the hotel owner Basil Fawlty, which earned him the 1980 British Academy Television Award for Best Entertainment Performance. He wrote and starred in *A Fish Called Wanda* (1988), and he won a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series for *Cheers* (1987).

American [[Jazz|jazz]] saxophonist, bandleader and composer, among the most influential figures in the history of jazz. Born in North Carolina, Coltrane moved to Philadelphia after high school and served in the Navy near the end of [[World War II]]. He saw [[Charlie Parker]] perform for the first time in 1945, and he worked in the bebop and hard bop idioms early in his career. He helped pioneer the use of modes and became one of the players at the forefront of free jazz. He recorded with [[Miles Davis]] and Thelonious Monk. His music took on an increasingly spiritual dimension, as shown on *A Love Supreme* (1965). Decades after his death he received numerous posthumous awards, including a special Pulitzer Prize, and he was canonized by the African Orthodox Church.

English Romantic landscape painter, known for revolutionizing the genre with pictures of Dedham Vale, the borderland of Suffolk and north [[Essex]]. He called the area "Constable Country" and invested his scenes with an intensity of affection. His best-known works include *Wivenhoe Park* (1816), *Dedham Vale* (1828) and *The Hay Wain* (1821). Although his paintings are now among the most valuable in British art, he was never financially successful, and he was elected to the Royal Academy at age 52. His work was embraced in France, where he sold more than in England and inspired the Barbizon school.

American businessman and philanthropist who founded the [[Standard Oil]] Company in 1870. He built it into a dominant force in oil refining, and by 1900 it controlled about 90% of the nation's oil production, making him the richest person in the United States. Critics argue that regulatory capture helped its [[Monopoly|monopoly]] power. In 1911 the Supreme Court ordered the company dismantled under federal antitrust laws, and it was broken up into 34 entities, including companies that became [[ExxonMobil]] and Chevron Corporation. In retirement he devoted his fortune to foundations that supported medicine, education and scientific research. He founded the [[University of Chicago]] and was a devout Baptist who abstained from alcohol and tobacco.
